title: Chapter 4.  Geography — Rivers, Lakes, Climate & Vegetation

blocks.content: This chapter completes the physical geography sequence by covering J&K's river systems (part of the wider Indus system), its famous lakes, and the sharply zoned climate and vegetation patterns that follow directly from the elevation gradient described in Chapter 1.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Himalayan rivers are perennial and glacier-fed, whereas Peninsular rivers are seasonal and rain-fed.
Chilika Lake in Odisha is India's largest brackish water lagoon, while Wular Lake in J&K is the largest freshwater lake.
The South-West Monsoon season (June to September) delivers the bulk of India's annual precipitation.
Tropical Deciduous Forests constitute the most dominant and widespread vegetation type across India.
West-flowing rivers like Narmada and Tapti flow through rift valleys and empty into the Arabian Sea forming estuaries.

blocks.content: J&K's rivers belong overwhelmingly to the Indus river system, and their management is governed internationally by the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) between India and Pakistan, which allocated the three 'Western Rivers' - Indus, Jhelum and Chenab - primarily to Pakistan's use (with India permitted specified non-consumptive/limited uses such as hydropower generation), while the three 'Eastern Rivers' - Ravi, Beas and Sutlej - were allocated to India.

The Jhelum River is the principal river of the Kashmir Valley, rising near Verinag in south Kashmir, flowing north-west through Srinagar and Wular Lake, before exiting through the Baramulla gorge towards Pakistan-administered territory and eventually joining the Chenab.

The Chenab River is the principal river of the Jammu division's mountainous districts (Doda, Kishtwar, Ramban), flowing through deep gorges and hosting several major hydroelectric projects; it is spanned by the Chenab Bridge, the world's highest railway arch bridge, part of the Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Rail Link (covered further in Chapter 23).
The Tawi River flows through Jammu city itself, a smaller but locally significant tributary system for the winter capital.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Indus Waters Treaty (1960): Western Rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) predominantly to Pakistan; Eastern Rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India. J&K's rivers (Jhelum, Chenab) are both 'Western Rivers' under this treaty - a frequently tested geography-cum-international-relations crossover fact, especially given periodic diplomatic tension over the treaty's implementation.

One of Asia's largest freshwater lakes; a natural flood-control basin for the Jhelum and an important wetland/bird habitat

blocks.content: J&K's climate varies dramatically with elevation and division: the Jammu plains experience a sub-tropical, monsoon-influenced climate with hot summers and the bulk of rainfall arriving via the South-West monsoon (July-September); the Kashmir Valley, shielded by the Pir Panjal from the full force of the monsoon, instead has a temperate climate with a more even, year-round precipitation pattern, including significant winter snowfall.

The Kashmir Valley experiences four distinct traditional seasons in local Kashmiri usage - Sonth (spring), Grishma (summer), Harud (autumn) and Wandah (winter) - each associated with characteristic agricultural and cultural activities, from spring blossom and autumn saffron-flowering to the deep winter 'Chillai Kalan' (the harshest 40-day cold spell of the Kashmiri winter calendar, typically from late December to end of January).
Higher-altitude and northern border areas approach alpine/cold-desert conditions similar to neighbouring Ladakh, particularly in areas like Gurez and the high passes.

cells: Even year-round precipitation; harsh winter cold spell 'Chillai Kalan' (~40 days, late Dec-Jan)
Extreme cold, low precipitation at highest elevations, glimpsing Ladakh-like conditions

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: 'Chillai Kalan' (the 40-day harshest winter period) is one of the most specific and frequently tested local-climate terms for the Kashmir Valley - remember it runs roughly from 21 December to 31 January, followed by shorter, milder cold spells locally called 'Chillai Khurd' and 'Chillai Bachha'.

items: Distinction between west-flowing rivers (Narmada, Tapti forming estuaries) and east-flowing rivers (Godavari, Mahanadi, Krishna, Cauvery forming deltas).
Coromandel Coast receives maximum rainfall during winter from the Retreating North-East Monsoon.
Identification of Ramsar Wetland Sites and major natural versus oxbow lakes.
The Jammu plains and Shivalik zone support tropical and sub-tropical dry deciduous forest, with sal and other broadleaf species in the lower foothills.

The mid-altitude zones (including much of the Kashmir Valley's surrounding slopes) support temperate coniferous forest - deodar (cedar), pine, fir and spruce are dominant, forming the basis of J&K's historically significant timber industry as well as its scenic hill-station landscapes (Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg).

Above the tree line (roughly 3,300-3,500 m upward), alpine meadows ('margs' in local Kashmiri terminology, as in Gulmarg - 'meadow of flowers' - and Sonamarg - 'meadow of gold') give way to bare rock, scree and permanent snow/glacier at the highest elevations.
The famous Kashmir saffron crop is cultivated specifically on the karewa terraces of the Pampore area (see Chapter 3), a unique agro-climatic niche found almost nowhere else in India.
Jhelum = principal river of Kashmir Valley (rises near Verinag, exits via Baramulla gorge); Chenab = principal river of Jammu's mountain districts.
Indus Waters Treaty (1960): J&K's main rivers (Jhelum, Chenab) are 'Western Rivers', predominantly allocated to Pakistan's use.
Wular Lake = largest freshwater lake (not Dal Lake, which is smaller but more famous); Dal Lake is Srinagar's iconic houseboat lake.
'Chillai Kalan' = the harshest 40-day Kashmir winter period (~21 Dec-31 Jan), followed by 'Chillai Khurd' and 'Chillai Bachha'.

Vegetation zones rise from tropical/sub-tropical deciduous (Jammu plains) -> temperate coniferous/deodar-pine forest (mid-altitude) -> alpine meadows ('margs', e.g. Gulmarg, Sonamarg) -> bare rock/snow.
